title: What is machine learning?
intro: What machine learning is, how it differs from plain programming — and why generalizing is the core idea.
keyPoints: Traditional programming: you write the rules. Machine learning: the computer learns the rules from examples (data + answers).
The definition: a program learns from experience E on task T, measured by performance P, if its performance on T improves.
Use ML for complex patterns, lots of data and a changing environment; use plain code for simple, explainable rules.
Learning = generalising: performing well on new, unseen data — not memorising training data.

sections.title: From writing rules to learning rules

blocks.html: Traditional programming: you write the rules (input → rules → output). Machine learning flips it: you supply examples with answers and the computer learns the rules itself.
Formally: a program learns from experience E for task T, measured by performance P, if its performance on T (measured by P) improves with E.
Spam filter example: T = classify e-mails, E = thousands of labeled examples, P = fraction correct. If you can name T, E and P, you have an ML problem.
ML shines when the pattern is complex (faces, speech), there is lots of data, and the environment changes (fraud adapts).
If the rule is simple and deterministic, plain code wins: faster, cheaper, explainable. And with little data a model rarely learns anything reliable.

blocks.html: A model can err and inherit bias from its data: always evaluate on unseen data and keep a human in the loop.
The goal is not to reproduce the training data but to generalize: predict well on data the model has never seen — learn patterns, not answers by heart.
In scikit-learn training is called fit. Perfect on training data but poor on new data is overfitting: memorizing instead of understanding.
Key sentence: a model that only performs well on data it has already seen has learned nothing.

sections.title: What kinds of problems does ML solve?

blocks.html: The two main tasks: predict a number (regression) or a category (classification); plus finding structure without labels (clustering).
